title: Common polynomial exponent for tractable digraph CSPs
formal: Does there exist an integer \(c\geq1\) such that, for every fixed finite digraph \(H\) for which \(\operatorname{CSP}(H)\) is in \(\mathrm P\), there are a deterministic algorithm \(M_{H}\) and a constant \(C_{H}\geq1\) that decide whether an input digraph \(G\) admits a homomorphism to \(H\) in at most \(C_{H}(L+1)^{c}\) bit steps, where \(L\) is the input encoding length? The exponent must be independent of \(H\), while both the machine and multiplicative constant may depend on \(H\).
why: The finite CSP dichotomy classifies each fixed set of local relations qualitatively. A common exponent would add a quantitative uniformity principle to this classification. Its failure would show that polynomial-time digraph CSPs can require arbitrarily large exponents even though every individual template is tractable.
status_note: The live author entry checked 15 September 2026 still poses the common-exponent question, with its own caveat that the list is not an exhaustive investigation. Checked the CSP dichotomy abstracts and the ICALP 2026 paper on the stronger uniform problem; bounded searches found no matching resolution of this exact target.

sentences: Each fixed finite digraph defines a constraint satisfaction problem through graph homomorphisms.
The question asks whether all polynomial-time cases can be solved with one common polynomial exponent.
The algorithm and its multiplicative constant may still depend on the fixed target digraph.
This is weaker than requiring one algorithm whose input includes an arbitrary target table.
A resolution would determine whether qualitative fixed-template tractability admits a shared quantitative time bound.

definitions:
A finite digraph \(G=(V_{G},E_{G})\) has a finite vertex set and a relation \(E_{G}\subseteq V_{G}\times V_{G}\); loops and both orientations of a pair are permitted. A homomorphism \(h:G\to H\) is a map such that \((u,v)\in E_{G}\) implies \((h(u),h(v))\in E_{H}\). It need not be injective or preserve nonedges. The problem \(\operatorname{CSP}(H)\) asks whether such a map exists. The target \(H\) is finite and nonempty, and is fixed before inputs are supplied. Including the empty target adds only a trivial decision problem and does not change existence of a common exponent.

Number the vertices of \(G\) by \(1,\ldots,n\), with \(n\geq0\). Encode \(n\) in unary followed by the number of listed edges in unary, each terminated by a zero, and then their endpoint pairs, with \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits per coordinate. Duplicate listed edges denote the same edge and still count toward the bit length \(L\); all labels must be valid. This representation counts isolated vertices. Algorithms reject malformed encodings. They are deterministic multitape Turing machines with finite programs and no oracle or advice; all reading, writing and intermediate bit operations count. Bounds are worst-case and answers must always be correct.

By \(\operatorname{CSP}(H)\in\mathrm P\) we mean existence of such a decider with a polynomial bound whose exponent may depend on \(H\). The question's quantifier order is \(\exists c\geq1\;\forall H\;\exists M_{H},C_{H}\), restricted to tractable \(H\), with correctness and the stated time bound for every input. No procedure producing \(M_{H}\) from \(H\) is required. The graph \(H\) is not part of the varying input or its length \(L\).

The author separately asks for one machine receiving \(G,H\), running in \(f(|H|)(L+1)^{c}\) time for a computable function \(f\) under the tractability promise. That fixed-parameter tractability assertion implies this card's assertion but is stronger. Polynomial time in the combined descriptions is stronger still. The inherited label “uniform” left these distinctions unresolved; this formulation recovers the main fixed-template source question.

The source permits conditional refutation by fine-grained assumptions. This card admits deterministic SETH as one explicitly specified assumption: for every real \(\delta>0\) there is an integer \(k\geq3\) such that Boolean \(k\)-SAT has no deterministic algorithm running in \(O(2^{(1-\delta)v}S^{d})\) time for any constant \(d\). Here \(v\) is the number of variables, \(S\) the explicit input bit length, and \(k\)-SAT asks satisfiability of a conjunction of clauses containing at most \(k\) signed Boolean variables. The assumption concerns worst-case inputs of unbounded size.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the common-exponent assertion or its negation. Following the source's express allowance, a Lean proof that deterministic SETH implies the negation is also an accepted answer and must be labelled conditional on SETH. No other unproved assumption is implicitly accepted. A negative answer must establish that for every proposed exponent \(c\), some tractable finite digraph template \(H\) has no correct deterministic \(O((L+1)^{c})\) decider, even with a template-specific machine and multiplicative constant. Refuting one algorithm or showing superpolynomial dependence on template size is insufficient. An affirmative proof need not give one algorithm receiving arbitrary template tables.

source_formulation.text: Is there one polynomial degree sufficient for every tractable fixed digraph CSP, with the template held fixed when input complexity is measured?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the main source question

context_blocks.text: A graph homomorphism assigns each input vertex a target vertex while respecting every directed edge. Holding the target fixed defines one decision problem. The finite CSP dichotomy says that each problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-complete, but the existence of separate polynomial algorithms does not itself supply a common exponent.

The question concerns a quantitative distinction within tractability: whether separate template-dependent polynomial degrees can always be replaced by a single constant. The programs and hidden multiplicative factors may remain different, and those factors need not be practical.

Bodirsky and Weiß’s 2026 paper studies the stronger question of time polynomial in both explicitly listed structures and its relationship to finding operations that preserve relations. Its introduction says this fully uniform problem is open even for important subclasses. That does not by itself prove that the weaker common-exponent problem here is open or false.

The source explicitly allows a fine-grained conditional lower bound. Such a result would have to establish unbounded input-exponent requirements among tractable templates, with each individual template fixed while its input graphs grow. A lower bound arising only because the target itself grows has different quantifiers.
